title: Signature Quiet Channel
body:
The Signature Quiet Channel is Manon's original design for team communication that never interrupts. Every message enters the channel with a topic, a needed action, and a reply window, and the channel holds messages until the reader opens them, instead of pushing alerts at people. Urgent items use a separate loud path that requires a reason code, so the quiet channel stays quiet by construction. The design's promise is simple: nobody's focus is spent by someone else's message without the sender paying the cost of declaring urgency.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part channel design. First, each message is tagged with its topic and its action, so readers can triage without opening everything. Second, reply windows are attached at send time, such as within one working day, and the channel sorts by window rather than by arrival. Third, the loud path is gated: sending loudly requires choosing a reason from a short list, and loud sends are counted per sender, so abuse is visible. Fourth, a weekly digest summarizes the quiet channel's decisions, so nobody must read every message to stay current. The demo sorts a small inbox by reply window and counts loud sends per sender.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature quiet channel. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 2026-10-25 loud - outage; 2026-10-26 quiet - budget; 2026-10-27 quiet - design; loud sends: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for teams whose chat tools currently interrupt everyone all day. Do not use it where genuine emergencies dominate the work, because a quiet-by-default channel would delay the very messages that matter most. Do not use it as a monitoring tool, because counting loud sends is for fairness, not for judging individuals. title: Signature One-Home Document
body:
The Signature One-Home Document is Manon's original design for shared documents that can never fork silently. Each document has exactly one home address in the Signature system, and every copy elsewhere is a live pointer to that home, not a separate file. When the home changes, every pointer shows the new version, and when someone tries to edit a pointer, the edit goes to the home. The design removes the most common document failure, two people improving two copies, by making a second copy structurally impossible.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-part home design. First, the home address is minted when the document is created and never changes, even if the title changes. Second, pointers carry the home address plus a cached title, and readers always resolve the pointer before reading, so stale reads cannot happen. Third, edits are applied only at the home, and the home keeps a dated change note for each edit, so the document's history is the home's history. The demo resolves three pointers to their homes and shows that two pointers to the same home always show the same version.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature one-home document. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: team guide -> guide-home shows v12; project plan -> plan-home shows v7; guide mirror -> guide-home shows v12 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for team plans, guides, and reference material that several people read and edit. Do not use it where offline copies are required, because pointers need the home to be reachable. Do not use it for documents that must be frozen and signed, where a fixed snapshot, not a live pointer, is the right artifact. title: Signature Passing Parcel
body:
The Signature Passing Parcel is Manon's original design for handoffs that cannot be dropped. A parcel wraps a piece of work with its state, its open items, its blockers, and its receiver, and the parcel is not considered passed until the receiver opens it and stamps it received. Until that stamp exists, the parcel stays on the sender's open list, visible to both. The design replaces hope, the belief that sending equals handing over, with a stamp, which is evidence that the handoff actually landed.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part parcel protocol. First, the sender packs the parcel with the work's state, open items, blockers, and deadline, using a fixed packing list so nothing is forgotten. Second, the parcel is addressed to a named receiver, never to a group, so one person is responsible for opening it. Third, the receiver opens the parcel and stamps it received, which moves it off the sender's open list and onto the receiver's. Fourth, parcels unopened past their reply window are escalated automatically to the team's shared board, so a silent receiver cannot silently stall the work. The demo packs two parcels and shows which one is still unstamped.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature passing parcel. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: launch page -> Ben : RECEIVED; support rota -> Cara : STILL OPEN; open parcels: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any transfer of responsibility where dropped handoffs have caused trouble before. Do not use it for trivial messages that need no confirmation, because stamping everything would drown the team in stamps. Do not use it to pressure receivers, because the escalation is to a shared board, not a punishment. title: Signature Decision Stone
body:
The Signature Decision Stone is Manon's original design for decisions that stay decided. Each decision is carved, in the design's language, as a stone: a small permanent entry holding the decision, the date, the decider, the options weighed, and the reason. Stones are laid in a path in date order, and later work links to the stone it follows. When someone asks why the team does something a certain way, the answer is a stone, not a memory. When new information arrives, a new stone can supersede an old one, but the old stone is never erased, so the path shows how thinking changed.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-field stone. First, the decision is stated in one sentence. Second, the date and decider are recorded. Third, the options weighed are listed, including the rejected option, so the stone shows a real choice. Fourth, the reason is written plainly, including any trade-off accepted. Fifth, the stone names what would supersede it, such as a new requirement or a measured result. The demo lays three stones and finds the one that answers a question about release days.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature decision stone. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: stones answering 'friday': [('2026-09-15', 'Releases ship on Fridays')] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for decisions that will outlive the meeting where they were made. Do not use it for trivial choices, because carving every small call would bury the important stones. Do not use it to lock in a bad decision, because superseding is part of the design, not a violation of it. title: Signature Duty Wheel
body:
The Signature Duty Wheel is Manon's original design for responsibility maps that stay honest. The wheel lists the team's tasks around its rim, and each task carries exactly one accountable name at its hub, with responsible names around it. A task with no hub name glows as unowned, and a task with two hub names refuses to close, because the design treats shared accountability for one task as no accountability. The wheel turns visibly when the team changes: names move, gaps appear, and the team fixes them before work drifts.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-rule wheel. First, every task on the rim gets exactly one hub name, the person who answers if the task fails. Second, responsible names are listed per task, and anyone consulted is listed only where their input changes the result. Third, the wheel is checked whenever membership or scope changes, and unowned tasks are assigned in that check, not left for later. Fourth, the wheel is displayed where the work is tracked, so ownership is visible to everyone, not filed away. The demo checks two tasks against the exactly-one-hub rule and reports the failures.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature duty wheel. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: launch page -> OK (one hub: Ben); support rota -> PROBLEM: 0 hubs Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for projects where ownership has been unclear or contested. Do not use it to load one person with every hub, because a wheel where one name holds all hubs shows overload, not ownership. Do not use it as a judgment tool about people, because its subject is tasks, not performance. title: Signature Request Gate
body:
The Signature Request Gate is Manon's original design for cross-team requests that never vanish. Every request passes through one gate carrying six fields: the outcome wanted, the reason, the deadline, the cost of waiting, the requester, and the receiving team. The gate stamps each request received, queues it visibly, and returns a position in the queue to the requester. Nothing enters the receiving team's work without passing the gate, and nothing at the gate is left unanswered: every request is accepted, queued, or declined with a reason and an alternative.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step gate protocol. First, the requester fills the six fields, stating the outcome rather than prescribing the method, so the receiving team can propose better ways. Second, the gate stamps the request and shows its queue position, so the requester can watch progress without chasing individuals. Third, triage runs on a visible schedule, and the queue order is public to both teams. Fourth, declined requests carry a reason and an alternative, and accepted requests carry a promised window. The demo triages a small queue by priority and prints the order.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature request gate. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: priority 1 - fix login bug; priority 2 - update docs; priority 3 - new report Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design wherever two teams depend on each other's work repeatedly. Do not use it for emergencies, where a direct escalation path must exist beside the gate. Do not use it as a wall, because a gate that declines everything is a refusal system wearing a gate's name. title: Signature Review Circle
body:
The Signature Review Circle is Manon's original design for reviews that teach instead of merely judging. Work enters the circle in small pieces, and each piece travels around reviewers who comment with reasons and suggested fixes, not bare verdicts. The author answers every comment, by changing the work or by explaining why not, and the circle closes only when every comment is answered. Review turnaround is measured in the open, and a piece that waits too long is lifted to the team's board, so review never becomes a quiet place where work stalls.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step circle. First, submissions are kept small, because small pieces get read and large ones get skimmed. Second, the author states what kind of review is wanted, such as correctness or clarity, so effort goes where it matters. Third, reviewers write comments that explain the concern and, where possible, offer a fix. Fourth, the author answers each comment in writing, so nothing is silently dropped. Fifth, turnaround is tracked, and overdue reviews are escalated visibly. The demo computes turnaround statistics from a small sample of review times.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature review circle. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: reviews: 5 average turnaround days: 2.0; overdue (over 3 days): 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any work product that benefits from a second pair of eyes. Do not use it as a substitute for testing against requirements, because review catches judgment errors, not every defect. Do not use it to slow urgent fixes, because emergency work needs a faster circle agreed in advance. title: Signature Memory Garden
body:
The Signature Memory Garden is Manon's original design for team knowledge that stays alive. Knowledge is planted as pages, each with an owner and a planted date, and pages age visibly: fresh pages are green, aging pages yellow, and pages past their review horizon turn brown and call for tending. Tending means updating or archiving, never ignoring, because a garden nobody tends becomes a wilderness where search returns dead answers. New joiners walk the garden first and note the bare patches, so gaps are found by fresh eyes rather than discovered in a crisis.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part garden loop. First, when someone answers a question others will ask again, the answer is planted as a page, not left in a private message. Second, each page carries its owner and its planted date, and age is computed openly. Third, new joiners tour the garden and report bare patches and confusing pages. Fourth, a tending round on a schedule updates or archives aging pages, so search keeps returning live answers. The demo ages four pages against a 180-day horizon and flags the ones needing tending.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature memory garden. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: onboarding guide -> green (12 days); server runbook -> BROWN - tend now (210 days); holiday policy -> green (45 days); old launch plan -> BROWN - tend now (400 days) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team whose knowledge lives mostly in people's heads. Do not use it as a dumping ground for every message, because an untended pile is as hard to search as no garden at all. Do not use it to replace mentoring, because some knowledge transfers only through working alongside someone. title: Signature Welcome Path
body:
The Signature Welcome Path is Manon's original design for onboarding as a guided walk rather than a document dump. The path is a sequence of small, real steps: access ready on day one, a named buddy, a first shippable task in week one, a tour of the team's stones and gardens in the first fortnight, and a thirty-day check-in that adjusts the path. Each step is stamped when done, and the path shows the newcomer and the team exactly where they stand, so nobody has to guess whether onboarding is on track.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step path. First, access and accounts are prepared before arrival, so day one is not lost to paperwork. Second, a buddy is named, a teammate whose job is to answer the questions a newcomer hesitates to ask twice. Third, the first task is small, real, and shippable within a week, so the newcomer learns the workflow by doing it. Fourth, the guided tour covers the team's decisions, documents, and current work, with the newcomer noting gaps. Fifth, the thirty-day check-in reviews progress and reshapes the remaining path. The demo reports path progress from a stamped step list.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature welcome path. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: welcome path: 3 of 5 steps stamped; remaining: ['first task shipped', '30-day check-in'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for every joiner, including internal transfers. Do not use it as a substitute for role training or professional qualifications, which the path complements but does not replace. Do not use it to measure a newcomer against a fixed speed, because people arrive with different backgrounds and the path should flex. title: Signature Loop Back
body:
The Signature Loop Back is Manon's original design for retrospectives that actually close. The loop opens by reviewing the previous loop's actions, one by one, marking each done, in progress, or dropped with a reason, before any new discussion starts. Only then does the team gather observations, name themes, and choose at most three new actions, each with an owner and a check date. Because the loop always opens on the last loop's promises, a team cannot quietly forget what it agreed, and participation stays high because input visibly becomes action.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step loop. First, previous actions are reviewed and closed honestly, including dropped actions with reasons. Second, data about the period is gathered from records, not memory alone. Third, observations are contributed in writing by everyone before discussion, so the loudest voice does not set the agenda. Fourth, themes are named and at most three actions are chosen, because ten actions mean none get done. Fifth, each action gets an owner and a check date and is tracked like any other work. The demo counts actions per owner from a small action list.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature loop back. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Ana owns 2 action(s); Ben owns 1 action(s) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team that repeats work in cycles. Do not use it to assign blame, because a loop that punishes honesty stops receiving honest input. Do not use it as a status meeting, because its purpose is learning and change, not reporting. title: Signature Talking Stick
body:
The Signature Talking Stick is Manon's original design for discussions that end in real decisions. The stick is a token, real or virtual, held by whoever is speaking, and only the holder speaks while others listen and note. Options are gathered before evaluation, scored visibly against agreed criteria, and disagreement is invited by name, with the facilitator asking who sees it differently and why. The decision is then stated with its trade-offs, and a stone is laid for it, so the group leaves with a call it can defend and a record it can revisit.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-step discussion design. First, the question is written down and agreed, so the group does not solve three problems at once. Second, options are gathered before any evaluation, so early judgment does not kill good ideas. Third, options are scored against agreed criteria in writing, making the comparison visible. Fourth, disagreement is invited explicitly and respectfully. Fifth, the group chooses, and the choice is stated with its trade-offs rather than dressed as unanimous when it is not. Sixth, the decision stone is laid with its reasons and its review trigger. The demo scores three options and names the winner.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature talking stick. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: options scored: {'keep tool A': 7, 'adopt tool B': 9, 'build in-house': 4}; winner: adopt tool B with 9 points Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for decisions where several reasonable people disagree and the outcome must hold. Do not use it for decisions one person is accountable for, where consultation is right but group agreement is not required. Do not use it to manufacture agreement where real disagreement remains, because a forced consensus collapses at the first difficulty. title: Signature Sun Clock
body:
The Signature Sun Clock is Manon's original design for distributed teams that refuse to meet at midnight. The clock shows every member's working window on one dial, converts local times to a shared reference honestly, and shades the whole-team overlap in gold. Overlap hours are reserved for decisions and unblocking, while status travels in writing. When membership or seasons change, the clock redraws itself and warns if the gold band has shrunk below the team's agreed minimum, so the team renegotiates its hours before anyone is quietly stranded in a midnight meeting.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step clock design. First, each member's window is recorded in local time with its offset, and conversions to the shared reference are computed, not guessed. Second, the whole-team overlap is computed as the latest start and earliest end across all windows. Third, the overlap is budgeted: decision meetings first, reviews second, and nothing else unless the team agrees. Fourth, the clock is redrawn on every membership or season change, and a shrinking gold band triggers a renegotiation. The demo converts three city windows to a shared clock and computes the overlap.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature sun clock. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: shared-clock windows: [('London', 9, 17), ('New York', 14, 22), ('Berlin', 8, 16)]; gold overlap: 14:00 to 16:00 (2 hours) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team spread across more than two time zones. Do not use it to justify always scheduling at the majority's convenience, because the burden of awkward hours should rotate or be shared. Do not use it where the team can work entirely in writing, because no overlap is needed when writing carries the work. title: Signature Shared Hearth
body:
The Signature Shared Hearth is Manon's original design for shared ownership that survives absence. The hearth is the team's owned thing, a service or project, kept warm by a rotation: at least two people are current on every critical part, a visible duty wheel spreads recurring load fairly, and changes are reviewed by someone other than the author so knowledge spreads through review itself. When a member leaves, the hearth does not go cold, because the warmth was never held by one person alone.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part hearth system. First, the owned thing and its boundaries are written down, so ownership is of something definite. Second, at least two people are current on every critical part, so absence never blocks the work. Third, a rotation spreads recurring load visibly and fairly, with swaps allowed but recorded. Fourth, changes are reviewed by someone other than the author. Fifth, ownership is reviewed when the team changes, because a hearth map naming departed members describes a team that no longer exists. The demo prints a four-week duty rotation.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature shared hearth. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: week 1 hearth keeper: Ana; week 2 hearth keeper: Ben; week 3 hearth keeper: Cara; week 4 hearth keeper: Dan Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for services or projects the team must keep running over time. Do not use it where a single accountable decision-maker is required, because shared ownership of a decision can blur accountability; pair it with a duty wheel for decisions. Do not use it as a way to avoid naming anyone, because shared ownership still needs named people on the rotation. title: Signature Many Hands Draft
body:
The Signature Many Hands Draft is Manon's original design for documents written by several people that still read as one voice. Contributors draft sections in parallel against one agreed outline, in the shared document rather than private copies, and one editor reads the assembled draft end to end for voice, consistency, and gaps. Versions are dated and summarized, so any reader can tell what changed and why, and the published version is frozen while a new draft begins. The design's rule is that the merge step protects every contribution: nothing is silently dropped, and every change is visible.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step drafting design. First, the outline is agreed by all contributors, including purpose, audience, and length, before drafting starts. Second, sections are assigned with owners and deadlines, and each section states its key facts up front so contradictions surface early. Third, drafts are written in the shared document, not in private copies. Fourth, one editor reads the assembled draft end to end and returns it for fixes. Fifth, versions are dated and summarized, and the published version is frozen. The demo counts unique contributions from an edit list, showing that repeated edits by one author on one section count once.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature many hands draft. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: unique contributions: 3 [('Ana', 'intro'), ('Ben', 'methods'), ('Cara', 'results')] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for reports, guides, and proposals written by more than one person. Do not use it for creative writing where a single voice is the point, or for legal documents where formal approval processes govern. Do not use it to let the loudest contributor overwrite others silently, because the merge step exists to protect every contribution. title: Signature Clear Water Review
body:
The Signature Clear Water Review is Manon's original design for learning from failures without blame. When something goes wrong, the team builds a timeline from records, names the contributing conditions, and asks what a reasonable, well-intentioned person would have done with the same information. Actions chosen must change the system, such as adding a check or clarifying ownership, rather than merely telling people to be more careful. The review is shared with the wider team, so the learning spreads, and its actions are tracked like any other work until they are done.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step review design. First, a timeline is built from records, in order, without relying on memory alone. Second, contributing conditions are named, including confusing tooling, missing checks, unclear ownership, and time pressure, alongside any human error. Third, the reasonable-person test separates system flaws from individual fault. Fourth, actions are chosen that change the system, and each gets an owner and a check date. Fifth, the review and its actions are shared beyond the room. The demo prints a sorted timeline and counts its events.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature clear water review. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 09:00 - deploy started; 09:12 - alert fired; 09:20 - rollback begun; 09:35 - service restored; events recorded: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design after any failure, outage, or near miss where the team wants the same thing not to happen again. Do not use it to excuse genuine misconduct, which belongs in a separate process, because conflating the two corrupts both. Do not use it as a report nobody reads, because a review without tracked actions is theater. title: Signature Team Promise Scroll
body:
The Signature Team Promise Scroll is Manon's original design for working agreements the team actually keeps. Promises are written as observable behaviors, such as reply within one working day or log every decision, and the scroll is kept where the work happens, not filed away. The team reviews the scroll at a fixed rhythm and updates it as the team changes, and breaches are raised kindly and early, against the scroll rather than against a person. Because the team wrote the scroll itself, defending it feels like keeping a promise, not obeying a rule.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part scroll process. First, the team discusses its real frictions and names the behaviors that help and the ones that hurt. Second, promises are written as observable behaviors, not vague aspirations. Third, the scroll is signed by the whole team and displayed where work happens. Fourth, the scroll is reviewed at a fixed rhythm, such as quarterly, and updated as the team changes. Fifth, breaches are raised early and kindly, against the scroll, so it stays a living tool. The demo scores a small promise list and names the promises needing improvement.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature team promise scroll. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: promises kept: 3 of 4; to improve: ['no meeting without an agenda'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any team that wants its collaboration norms explicit instead of assumed. Do not use it as a disciplinary document, because a scroll enforced as a rulebook loses the consent that makes it work. Do not use it to freeze norms that should evolve, because the review rhythm is part of the scroll, not an optional extra.
